Today is the thirteenth lecture, focusing on matters related to tendering and the construction process. These details may seem trivial, but as the general contractor, you should be quite familiar with them.

First, the tasks we need to complete as electrical consultants during the tendering phase include: preparing a comprehensive tender package before the tendering begins, which should contain drawings, technical specifications, and sometimes a budget estimate. This budget will serve as the client’s reserve price or basis for the tender.

Generally, tendering can be divided into two forms: open tendering and invited tendering. For large-scale or government projects, during open tendering, we as consulting advisors need to attend the tender meeting, known as Job Showing. The tender document package includes technical documents and tender documents. Bidders can raise questions regarding the Scope of Work and technical aspects to the consulting advisors during the Job Showing stage. It is important to note that on-site answers should not be considered formal responses; final confirmation must be provided in writing.

The main purpose of Job Showing is to introduce the project overview to bidders and address their queries, which differs from the domestic construction briefing. Construction briefings usually take place after tendering is completed and before construction begins, primarily addressing technical or scope-related questions raised by the Contractor.

Additionally, after the tendering process begins, a Reply to RFI (Request for Information) window period is established. The duration of this window depends on the project scale, typically ranging from three to four weeks. Large projects such as CPD projects may have longer periods, while smaller projects may require only one week. During this period, questions raised by contractors after reviewing the tender documents must be answered through formal channels.

These issues encompass not only technical or scope of work matters but also various problems arising during project execution, such as contractual or on-site construction issues. All such matters will be formally raised. Many of these may be irrelevant to the Electrical Consultant, with our primary focus being on scope of work and technical aspects.

These questions will be officially submitted through RFIs, after which the client will forward them to the consultant. The consultant will provide formal responses, which could range from simple emails to official letterhead replies. For clearer communication, drawings or sketches may be attached when necessary.

Furthermore, as the tender process nears completion, the client will collect submitted bids or proposals from contractors. The client will conduct their own review while also engaging the consultant to evaluate them, focusing particularly on scope of work and technical issues, along with assessing contractor qualifications including their background, reputation, and suitability for project requirements. The client will also review insurance, safety clearances, and contract terms.

Upon completing the evaluation, the consultant will submit a Recommendation Letter to the client, providing professional advice based on the assessment of bidder proposals.

Upon completing the evaluation, the consultant will submit a Recommendation Letter to the client, providing professional advice based on the assessment of bidder proposals.

Of course, we don’t have the authority to decide the ownership of projects, but we can provide some recommendations. It’s important to note that not all projects are required to follow these suggestions. The first three items are mandatory tasks for consultants, while the fourth one depends on specific circumstances.

In North America, particularly in Canada, government projects must follow specific procedures. Articles 4 and 5 are actually interconnected. After the bidding process concludes, we gather all RFIs (Requests for Information) and handle supplementary documents (Addenda). Once bidding is completed, the project moves into the construction phase, at which point we issue IFC (Issued for Construction) documents. IFC files include IFT documents along with all modifications and clarifications from the bidding process, covering technical revisions, scope of work adjustments, and other clarifications.

However, projects can sometimes stall due to funding issues, especially government projects and certain private initiatives. Even if the bidding process has been finalized, a project might be revived after a year or two, requiring a retender, which repeats the entire bidding procedure.
Construction Administration during the construction process is similar to what is commonly known as construction supervision.

Next, we will discuss Construction Administration during the construction process, which is similar to what you may know as construction supervision.

As consultants in North America, our work under the CEA (Consulting Engineering Agreement) overlaps significantly with construction supervision in terms of scope and technical aspects. However, in contract management and commercial matters, the consultant’s involvement may not be as extensive as that of a construction supervisor.

After this presentation, we welcome discussions on the similarities and differences between the roles and responsibilities of North American consultants in Construction Administration and construction supervision in Egypt, China, or other countries.

During the construction phase, we need to clarify the scope of work and its execution methods, and discuss the differences in responsibilities of electrical consultants across regions such as North America, China, and Egypt during this stage.

In previous lessons, we have thoroughly explained the content related to Construction Administration. This session will primarily focus on a systematic summary. In North America, not all projects are required to undergo Construction Administration. However, from a technical responsibility perspective, as consultants and engineers, we are accountable for the entire project. While specific scopes of work may vary, the technical responsibilities are clearly defined.

During the Construction Administration process, we may assist clients with commercial activities such as price reviews or contract examinations, but these tasks are not mandatory. On the technical side, matters like contract clause issues or project modifications require our full participation. This portion of work can be included in the initial contract or exist as a separate agreement.

The design phase can adopt a Lump Sum contract approach, while the Construction Administration phase can similarly use either a Lump Sum or Time and Material billing model. In Canada, the construction contract signed between owners and contractors is called the CCDC contract. For government projects, we may need to assist with CCDC contract printing services, but our primary responsibility lies in reviewing technical documentation. The CCDC contract constitutes a comprehensive construction contract package containing numerous technical documents and materials we must provide as consultants, though this task is not compulsory.

During the construction phase, we need to regularly attend construction meetings, with the specific frequency determined by the Construction Administration clauses in the contract. Sometimes we are required to chair the meetings, while other times we only need to participate.

Additionally, the construction phase involves RFIs (Request for Information). Although contractors also raise questions during the bidding phase, the focus then is primarily on broad Scope of Work issues for pricing purposes. In contrast, RFIs during the construction phase are more focused on on-site technical issues. We can address these through formal RFI responses, sometimes supplemented with sketches. Later, I will provide some sample documents for reference.

Another critical aspect is issuing Site Instructions. When the client, consultants, or contractors request modifications or raise issues, we may need to issue site instructions. These instructions may or may not lead to a Change Order. If the issue is merely a clarification (Classification), it typically does not result in adjustments to the contract price. However, if it involves a Scope of Work Change, it may trigger a Change Order or a CCN (Contract Change Notice). Whenever there are changes to the contract or scope of work, we must promptly issue a CCN.

In the coordination work of the previous lesson, the coordination content between the electrical discipline and other disciplines was already mentioned. Regarding the process, for example, Site Instructions (SI) and R5 may trigger Scope Work Changes (SWC). Once all parties confirm this as a contract variation, as the consultant, a Contemplated Change Notice (CCN) will be issued. This is a formal document used to notify the contractor of the change details. The CCN will clearly specify the scope of work or specific modification requirements.

After the contractor submits a quotation based on the CCN, since the client usually lacks a technical team for review, the quotation will be forwarded to the consultant for evaluation of its reasonableness. If the quotation is reasonable and approved by the client, it will form a Change Order (CO); if unreasonable, it will be returned for revision until an agreement is reached. The Change Order may be prepared by the consultant on behalf of the client or completed independently by the client’s team.

Additionally, the contractor’s Progress Claim must also be reviewed. The contractor submits monthly invoices and construction progress reports to the client. After the consultant’s approval, a Certificate of Payment (COP) will be issued, confirming the progress as reasonable and recommending the client to release the payment.

During the construction process, the Client typically withholds 10% of the payment to the contractor. This portion of the payment is usually released 45 days after substantial completion of the project. The specific criteria for substantial completion will be explained in detail later.

Additionally, regular on-site inspections are required during the construction phase, and inspection reports must be submitted to the Client. If any issues are identified during inspections, they will be promptly communicated to the contractor. Any technical issues requiring modification or resolution will also be addressed accordingly.

After the substantial completion inspection, relevant letters or certificates need to be prepared. As mentioned in previous courses, this is a critical milestone and also a legal document. Issuing this document signifies that the project has reached substantial completion. Associated with this is a deficiency list, which details the specific items requiring rectification.

From a contractual perspective, once the contractor receives this letter, they can invoice the owner for the majority of the contract amount, and the owner is obligated to make the corresponding payment. Meanwhile, the owner can use this document to apply for an occupancy certificate from municipal authorities, indicating that the project has achieved substantial completion. The substantial completion letter must be signed and stamped by the engineer.

After completing the substantial completion inspection, consultants must prepare a deficiency list. During commissioning activities, consultants are required to conduct on-site supervision (LWX) but are not required to be present for the entire process; they may selectively observe specific testing phases. Commissioning is typically carried out by a commissioning agent or commissioning authority, who submits a commissioning report upon completion. Consultants must review this report and provide comments.

Once all deficiencies have been rectified, a final completion inspection must be conducted. At this stage, consultants perform on-site verification and issue a final completion certificate.

If all these tasks have been completed, the as-built drawings must still be addressed. In practice, contractors make modifications to the drawings during the construction process.

If all these tasks have been completed, we still need to handle the as-built drawings. In reality, contractors make modifications to the drawings during the construction process.

The contractor must mark the changes on paper drawings with red ink. According to contract terms, sometimes the contractor is required to provide old versions of as-built drawings in CAD format, but usually, the consultant is responsible for creating the CAD version.

The consultant must also review the paper as-built drawings marked by the contractor and promptly point out any issues if found.

During the project closeout phase, we need to review the Operation and Maintenance Package provided by the contractor. This package includes all technical and contractual documents of the project, such as as-built drawings, operation and maintenance manuals, approved drawings, contractor information, warranty documents, commissioning records, and training logs, which must be compiled into a complete package.

Typically, junior staff lack relevant experience during construction, so such tasks are often handled by intermediate or senior employees. For large projects, an on-site team or dedicated personnel must be assigned to handle Construction Administration work, whose responsibilities are similar to those of a supervisor. Specific arrangements depend on the agreement budget. In North America, Construction Administration fees account for approximately 35% of design fees due to the extensive workload involved.

For example, in a typical project with a total cost of 100 units, 60 units are allocated to design, 5 units to bidding services, and 35 units to Construction Administration. This provides a basic understanding of the cost distribution.

In a typical project with a total cost of 100 units, 60 units are allocated to design, 5 units to bidding services, and 35 units to construction administration. This provides a basic understanding of the cost distribution.

As previously discussed at Jiyang, there are differences between North American CEA and supervisors in other regions. While North American construction administration overlaps significantly with supervision, supervisors may take on more responsibilities in contract management and project schedule control compared to North American consultants. North American consultants primarily focus on clarifying the scope of work, providing technical support, and assisting the owner in reviewing progress reports and quotations.

Regarding the siting inspection, we are only responsible for technical quality-related work. Schedule management, contract disputes, and safety management are not within our scope of responsibility; these should be handled by the on-site supervision team.

Below I will share some differences between North America and China in the construction industry from a personal perspective. Having left China over twenty years ago, my understanding of the current domestic situation is limited, so I welcome any corrections if there are inaccuracies.

North America has more comprehensive documentation management and standardized processes, placing greater emphasis on quality and safety. However, project timelines are relatively slower, and costs are higher. Based on earlier data, project durations in North America were about five times longer than in China, with costs also five times higher. As living standards and incomes in China have risen, this gap may have narrowed somewhat.

In terms of operational models, North America typically employs Project Managers and Consultants. During the construction phase, there is a Construction Manager, who may be appointed by the owner or the general contractor, along with an independent commissioning agent. Additionally, the roles of general contractors and subcontractors are clearly defined. North America extensively uses specialized software for construction management, including schedule and contract management.

In the industrial sector, the EPC or EPCM model (Engineering, Procurement, Construction, and Management) is adopted, primarily for large-scale industrial projects. However, in the commercial sector, consultants and contractors are usually separate entities. Currently, in the U.S. and Canada, pure EPC models are less common, with EPCM being more widely used. For example, in the oil and gas industry, engineering companies mainly handle EPCM, while construction is undertaken by large construction firms.

Other operational models will be discussed in detail in the final session. Next, I will present some documentation from North American construction phases for your reference.

But as a component designed for long-term steady-state operation, the wire has strong transient overload capability. Taking a wire with a 70-ampere current-carrying capacity as an example, the current may momentarily reach 150 amperes during startup, but this lasts only 1-2 minutes, which will not damage the wire.

Therefore, wire selection does not need to be overly conservative. The tripping characteristics of the switch and the short-term overload capability of the wire are two independent design considerations.

In North America, motor protection is divided into two parts: motor protection and circuit protection. Motor protection typically consists of thermal trips and contactors, corresponding to North American Motor Starters or MCCs, primarily used for overload protection of low-voltage motors. As for circuit protection, North America employs two types of circuit breakers: magnetic trip and thermal trip, or a combination of both. Thermal trip circuit breakers inherently provide overload protection.

For motor circuits, the circuit breaker must provide both overload and short-circuit protection. If a motor starter is already configured for motor protection, the circuit protection primarily focuses on the conductors, addressing overload and short-circuit scenarios. During a short circuit, the circuit breaker trips at 10 to 15 times the rated current, while overload protection is achieved through the thermal element, safeguarding the circuit rather than the motor itself.

During selection, if sized at 125% (e.g., a 100-amp breaker for an 80-amp load current), the 1.25 overload protection factor does not apply to motor circuits. Motor starting current can exceed twice the rated current, yet the breaker will not trip. Therefore, North American standards specify that motor circuit breakers have an overload protection setting of 12.5 times the frame size, while the short-circuit protection multiplier is determined case by case.

This design is based on the unique characteristics of motor loads. Unlike lighting or heating loads, motors come with built-in overload protection devices (e.g., Motor Starters). When a motor is overloaded, its own protection device should activate, not the upstream breaker. Hence, North American standards adopt this specialized configuration for motor circuit protection.

The selection must be made according to the 2.5 times standard. If using a motor-type protective circuit breaker, simply follow this standard for selection. It is necessary to refer to local Egyptian regulations to confirm if there are any special requirements, as long as it complies with local standards. In North America, this standard is followed.

Next, we will explain the construction drawings, which are the main focus of this course.

Actually, many details don’t need to be elaborated one by one—everyone is quite clear about them.

The components included in shop drawings are actually quite extensive. For example, datasheet specifications involve detailed information about equipment, materials, systems, and other aspects. As a contractor, a substantial amount of materials must be prepared, while as a consultant engineer, it is necessary to clarify which shop drawings need to be submitted, what content requires review, and the depth of review during the design phase. In North America, there are no strict regulatory requirements in this regard—it is entirely up to the electrical engineer’s understanding of the system and the project’s quality control standards. The specifications do not impose many mandatory rules.

During the review process, the engineer has considerable discretionary authority. Even if certain materials are submitted with poor quality or not submitted at all, the final decision ultimately depends on the consultant’s judgment. As a result, different consultants may have varying standards of strictness in engineering projects. Typically, younger or more meticulous consultants will demand more detailed materials, while experienced ones may be relatively lenient. This entirely depends on individual working styles.

For certain large-scale equipment and standardized materials, the review requirements are relatively straightforward. For instance, pipeline materials only require confirmation of basic parameters before approval for procurement. However, for critical equipment such as high and low voltage switchgear, transformers, generators, UPS, etc., strict review by the engineer is mandatory. From a consulting perspective, we dedicate more effort to such equipment, focusing on dimensions, environmental adaptability, electrical parameters, certifications, and other key aspects. For conventional materials like lighting fixtures and wiring, the review process is simpler.

It is particularly important to note that certain systems, such as BAS (Building Automation System) and FA (Fire Alarm) systems, fall under the scope of detail design rather than traditional shop drawings. Reviews for such systems require greater precision and expertise.

He typically conducts highly detailed designs, such as BAS fire alarm and security systems, all of which come with comprehensive design drawings.

In a narrow sense, Shop Drawings refer to the detailed drawings used for factory fabrication. However, the industry has widely adopted this term, so it remains in use today. In reality, there is a broader term called Summito, which encompasses technical documents submitted by consultants and sometimes includes contract-submitted shop drawings.

Additionally, system support documents may also need to be submitted, such as HT (Hitrace). Such requirements are less common in civil and commercial projects and are primarily applied in industrial sectors, especially outdoor industrial projects involving extensive piping.

Shop drawing reviews for aspects like winter pipeline insulation are particularly critical, as they effectively ensure construction quality.

Shop drawing reviews for aspects like winter pipeline insulation are particularly critical, as they effectively ensure construction quality. Moreover, they help prevent disputes or legal issues during the construction phase. From both the consultant’s and contractual perspectives, shop drawings hold significant importance. In essence, they serve as a technical or quality-oriented purchase agreement. When contractors face challenges, they can defend their work based on submitted and approved shop drawings. As engineers, reviewing these drawings ensures technical accuracy, thereby guaranteeing construction quality.

From the owner’s standpoint, shop drawings help safeguard project quality and provide a foundation for future operations and maintenance. In cases of equipment failure or troubleshooting, these drawings serve as reliable references for technical specifications. During construction and commissioning phases, reviewing shop drawings is particularly critical. If issues arise during commissioning or testing, stakeholders can trace the root cause—whether it stems from design flaws, manufacturing defects, or errors in transportation and installation—using the drawings as traceable documentation.

The following section will detail the types of shop drawings specific to the electrical discipline.

Broadly speaking, all electrical systems, equipment, and materials used during the project require the submission of Shop Drawings for approval. Additionally, design-related content such as software design solutions—including Sequence of Operation (SOO), Programming, and Graphics—must also be submitted. Specific requirements, including submission content, level of detail, and submission methods (electronic or hard copy), are clearly outlined in the Project Specifications.

In North America, project specifications are divided into Front-End Specifications, which encompass general requirements under Division Zero and Division One, as well as detailed requirements for specific equipment sections such as transformers, generators, and high/low-voltage switchgear. Engineers must clearly define their technical and quality control needs for the project to determine the content and depth of shop drawings required from contractors. Contractors should thoroughly review the engineer’s specifications early in the construction phase to identify the types and level of detail required for shop drawings, rather than relying solely on experience, as requirements vary from project to project.

- Bulk Materials and Standard Devices, which refer to widely used materials or relatively simple electrical equipment such as lighting fixtures, wires, cables, conduits, switches, outlets, and grounding materials.

These shop drawings are relatively straightforward, requiring only the extraction and submission of relevant information from manufacturers or product selections. Any uncertainties can be clarified with the electrical engineer through an RFI (Request for Information).

Regarding the review content of shop drawings, I will provide an overview from the perspective of a consultant. As consultants, our primary focus when reviewing shop drawings is identifying discrepancies between them and the design documents (including drawings and specifications). Performance exceeding requirements is acceptable, but anything below standards will not be approved.

Key review points include:

Electrical parameters must strictly comply with design requirements, such as voltage (single-phase/three-phase), current, power factor, and interrupting capacity. For example, using 80A when the drawing specifies 100A, or selecting single-phase instead of three-phase, is unacceptable.

Manufacturer selection must adhere to specifications, including model numbers and quantities. Sufficient spare capacity must also be verified.

Insulation type/level is critical for high-voltage equipment. Transformer temperature rise and noise levels must be checked, as generators also have noise considerations.

Material selection must meet requirements—for instance, the choice between copper and aluminum conductors directly impacts power loss and lifespan. Transformer winding materials are particularly crucial.

Equipment type must be confirmed, such as whether generators are diesel or gas-powered.

Physical dimensions are vital, especially for large equipment like generators, transformers, and switchgear. Substituting a different manufacturer’s larger-sized product may cause installation issues.

All deviations from design documents must be clearly identified and corrected.

All deviations from design documents must be clearly identified and corrected.

This is a frequently occurring issue, which has been reported multiple times and constitutes a major design or engineering flaw. If such a situation arises, the inability to install the equipment will lead to serious problems.

Another critical issue is the arrangement of incoming and outgoing lines, such as top entry, bottom entry, or side entry, which is particularly important when connecting to the local power grid. Additionally, the installation method (wall-mounted or floor-standing) must be confirmed in advance.

For example, if a small transformer originally intended for wall-mounted installation is mistakenly configured for floor-standing use and lacks wall-mounting accessories, it will cause significant inconvenience.

For example, if a small transformer originally intended for wall-mounted installation is mistakenly configured for floor-standing use and lacks wall-mounting accessories, it will cause significant inconvenience.

Environmental requirements are equally important, such as insulation class. If the equipment is supposed to be installed outdoors, it must be equipped with corresponding outdoor protection measures.

Improper handling of interior components may lead to issues such as rust or aging, which is unacceptable. For UPS generators or battery systems, special attention must be paid to their backup time, which must comply with local electrical codes. If the nominal backup time of a selected battery is two hours but it can only sustain one hour in practice, this does not meet the requirements.

During the construction drawing design phase, coordination is required for equipment selection related to other disciplines. For example, equipment such as elevators or ventilation systems involved in mechanical or architectural disciplines may have final selections that differ from the mechanical parameters assumed during the design phase. When significant changes occur in equipment power requirements, the power distribution scheme must be re-evaluated, potentially necessitating the replacement of entire distribution panels or reconfiguration of circuit breaker settings.

Coordination with the mechanical discipline is particularly critical. When reviewing construction drawings for equipment such as air handling units or pumps provided by them, it is essential to confirm whether disconnect switches, controllers, or variable frequency drives (VFDs) are included. Construction drawing reviews should not be limited to one’s own discipline but must also include drawings of related equipment from other disciplines.

Furthermore, all equipment and materials must meet NEMA standards and the specifications of local Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJs). Special projects (e.g., laboratories, hospitals, nuclear facilities) may have additional technical requirements that must be thoroughly considered by consultants during the construction drawing review phase.

After the review process is completed, there are typically several possible outcomes:

After the review process is completed, there are typically several possible outcomes:

“Reviewed/approved without comments”, indicating that the construction drawings fully meet the requirements and can be directly used for ordering and production.

“Reviewed/approved with comments”, meaning there are minor issues with the drawings that do not require resubmission but should be corrected in subsequent work.

“Rejected with comments resubmitted”, signifying that the drawings contain major errors or were not submitted according to design requirements, necessitating the identification of key issues and return for revision.

The review of construction drawings must include the reviewer’s name, date, and a disclaimer. The review comments should cover the following:

Incorrect, missing, or inconsistent elements in the drawings;

Deviations from the design requirements;

Clear instructions on how the drawings should be modified.

For routine and simple Shop Drawings, junior staff can handle the review. However, for complex or critical equipment Shop Drawings, it is advisable to assign senior personnel. Especially in large-scale projects like the CPD Project, balancing time and quality is essential when reviewing Shop Drawings. As a consulting firm, engineers must possess efficient reading skills to ensure timely completion of reviews.

It is important to note that Shop Drawing reviews are not limited to our team; other stakeholders such as the client or third parties may also participate.
